text:
Recent work supports measuring history dependence through interventions. [Klenitskiy et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) compare original and shuffled histories across 15 datasets, finding weak sequential structure in several popular benchmarks. [Liu et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) distinguish arbitrary shuffling from shuffling constrained by item availability: apparent sequential signal can reflect catalog timing as well as user behavior. [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) show that simple recency-weighted pairwise models can outperform Transformer reproductions on several benchmarks, supporting last-item and additive-history controls before attributing gains to complex sequence modeling.

Practical diagnostic proposal: freeze model weights, training prefixes, targets, candidates and exclusion masks; compare intact predictions with the residual contribution disabled, equal-size recent versus older deletions, random deletions, and repeated count-preserving shuffles. Include shuffling that preserves the last item to separate earlier-order dependence from last-item sensitivity. Report paired target-rank changes, HR@10 changes and top-10 turnover, defined as 1−|intersection|/10; compare with uniform-history aggregation, last-item and training-popularity controls. Stratify by category, prefix length and target training frequency, with paired uncertainty estimates. These are proposed measurements, not reported benchmark results.

Interpret changes as model reliance under specified interventions. [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) explicitly study recency-bias measurement; recency sensitivity alone does not establish harmful bias. Deleting inputs can also change positions and create unfamiliar histories, while disabling a residual measures its contribution within the trained model rather than the performance of a retrained alternative. Neither intervention establishes causal user intent or unobserved conformity traits.
